lessons.title: What Is Artificial Intelligence?
lessons.description: A plain explanation of AI, how it differs from machine learning and deep learning, and a hands-on exercise that compares a rule-based filter with one that learns from examples.

content.text: Artificial intelligence, or AI, is software that does tasks we normally think need human judgement. Recognising a face in a photo, translating a sentence, recommending a job, spotting a fake message, or writing a paragraph are all examples. AI is not one single technology. It is a broad label that covers many different techniques, some very old and some very new. In this first lesson you will learn what the main words mean, see the difference between a program that follows rules and a program that learns, and build a small example of both so that you can see the difference with your own eyes.

You do not need any maths or programming knowledge to follow the ideas. If you can read a short piece of TypeScript code you will get more from the exercise, but the explanations are written in easy English, and every idea comes with an example from everyday life or from job hunting.
AI, machine learning and deep learning

You will see three terms again and again: AI, machine learning and deep learning. They are nested, like a set of boxes. **AI** is the biggest box: any software that appears to show intelligent behaviour. **Machine learning**, often shortened to ML, is a smaller box inside it. In machine learning the program is not given the rules. Instead it is shown many examples, and it works out a pattern by itself. **Deep learning** is a still smaller box inside machine learning. It uses neural networks with many layers, and it is the technology behind most of the AI news you read today, including chat assistants such as Claude.

A simple way to remember the difference is to think about how you would teach a new person to spot a fake job message. You could write a list of rules on a card: “If the message asks for money before the job starts, it is fake.” That is the **rule-based** way. Or you could show the person two hundred real messages and two hundred fake ones, and let them develop a feeling for the difference without writing any rules down. That is the **learning** way. Both can work. They fail in different ways, and a good engineer knows when to use each.
Rule-based systems

A rule-based system is a program where a human writes the logic. A resume checker that says “this resume has no email address” is a rule-based system. A rule is easy to read, easy to explain and easy to fix. If a user asks, “Why was my message flagged?”, you can point to the exact rule. Rule-based systems are also very predictable. The same input always gives the same output.

The weakness is that rules only cover what the writer thought of. Scammers change their words every week. If your rule looks for the phrase “registration fee”, a scammer will write “processing charge” instead, and your rule sees nothing. To keep up you must keep adding rules by hand, and the list gets long and hard to manage.
Learning systems

A learning system works in the opposite way. You give it examples that are already labelled, such as “this message is a scam” and “this message is normal”. The program counts and measures things in those examples and builds a small mathematical model. When a new message arrives, the model uses what it learned to guess. Nobody wrote a rule about “processing charge”. But if the word “charge” appeared often in scam examples and rarely in normal ones, the model will lean towards “scam” whenever it sees that word.

This is powerful because the model can notice patterns that a person did not think of. It is also risky, for three reasons. First, the model is only as good as its examples. If your examples are few, old or one-sided, the model will be poor or unfair. Second, it is harder to explain: the answer comes from many small numbers rather than one clear rule. Third, it can be wrong with confidence. A learning system will happily give an answer even for a message that looks nothing like its examples.
Narrow AI and general AI

Every AI product you can use today is **narrow AI**. It is very good at a limited set of tasks and useless outside them. A resume parser does not drive a car, and a chess engine cannot write a cover letter. Even large language models, which can do many different language tasks, are still narrow in an important way: they work with text and patterns in text, and they have no goals of their own. **General AI**, a system that can do any intellectual task a person can do, is a research goal. It is not a product you can buy or a thing you need to worry about when you build today’s apps.
Where you already meet AI

items: **Spam filters** decide which emails go to the junk folder. Most use a learning method.
**Search and recommendations** decide which jobs, videos or products you see first.
**Speech to text** on your phone turns your voice into words.
**Applicant tracking systems (ATS)** read resumes, pull out skills and rank candidates. Some use rules, some use learning, and many use both.
**Chat assistants** such as Claude write, summarise and explain in plain language.

content.text: What AI cannot do well

Knowing the limits is as useful as knowing the strengths. AI systems learn from data, so poor data gives poor results. If a hiring model learned from past decisions that were unfair, it will copy the unfairness. AI can be confidently wrong. It does not understand the world the way people do. And for decisions that matter, such as hiring, health or money, a person should check the result. Keep one habit from this lesson for the whole course: whenever you read about an AI feature, ask two questions. What data did it learn from? And what happens when it is wrong?

They show how the ideas work, but they are not real language models.
Your task: rules against learning

In this task you will build the first page of the lab. It lets you type a job message and see two verdicts side by side: one from a few hand-written rules, and one from a small model that learns from labelled examples.
**What you will build**

items: A list of 14 example messages, each marked as a scam or as normal.
Four hand-written rules, for example “asks you to pay first” and “pushes you to hurry”.
A small learning model called naive Bayes. It counts how often each word appears in scam and in normal examples, and turns those counts into a score.
An Angular page with a text box, two result cards, and buttons to add your own examples.

content.text: **Steps**

items: Create src/app/lib/spam.ts. Define the type Example with a text and a spam flag, and write the 14 starting examples (7 scam, 7 normal). Use realistic messages: scam ones mention fees, OTP codes or guaranteed income, and normal ones mention interviews and documents.

Write the rules as a list of objects, each with a name and a test function that checks the text with a regular expression. Write ruleVerdict, which runs all rules and returns the names of the rules that fired.

Write the NaiveBayes class. In the constructor, count for every word how many scam and how many normal examples contain it. Write weight(word) so that a positive number pushes towards scam and a negative number pushes towards normal. Add one to every count so that a word never seen in one group does not give a zero.
Write classify(text). Add the weights of the known words in the message to a starting value (the prior) and turn the total into a probability between 0 and 1 with the formula 1 / (1 + e^-x).

Create the page in src/app/pages/spam.ts. Show the message box, both verdicts, the rules that fired, and the words that pushed the learned verdict the most. Add buttons to add the current message as a scam example or as a normal example, and rebuild the model each time.

items: Make the words lower case and count each word once per message. Otherwise a long message with a repeated word gets too much influence.
Use Set to remove repeated words from a message.
Keep the logic in lib/spam.ts, with no Angular code, so that you can test it on its own.
Try a clever scam sentence that uses none of your rule words. Then add it as an example and see what changes.

Try to build it yourself first. Struggling with the first version is where the understanding grows. Then compare with the solution below.

What you learned

items: AI is a broad label. Machine learning is the part where programs learn patterns from examples. Deep learning is machine learning with many-layered neural networks.
A rule-based system is predictable and easy to explain, but it only covers what a person thought of.
A learning system can notice patterns nobody wrote down, but it depends on its examples and is harder to explain.
Today’s AI is narrow. It does limited tasks well and needs human checking when the stakes are high.

content.text: In the next lesson you will meet the small set of maths ideas that sit behind almost everything in AI: vectors, similarity, averages, probabilities and learning by small steps.

faqs.q: Is machine learning the same as AI?
faqs.a: No. Machine learning is one approach inside AI, where programs learn patterns from data. AI also includes older rule-based methods.

faqs.q: Do I need advanced maths to start learning AI?
faqs.a: Not to use and build with AI tools. A few basic ideas, such as averages and similarity, help you understand how models work. The next lesson covers them with simple examples.

faqs.q: Should I use rules or learning for my own project?
faqs.a: Use rules when the logic is clear, must be explained, or must never change, for example a legal check. Use learning when the patterns are too many or too fuzzy to write down. Many real systems combine both.

faqs.q: Is the naive Bayes model in this lesson a real AI?
faqs.a: Yes, it is a real and still widely used machine learning method, especially for spam filtering. It is simple, which makes it a good first example. Large language models are far bigger and work differently.

lessons.title: Maths and Statistics You Need for AI
lessons.description: The small set of maths ideas behind AI: vectors, similarity, averages, probability and learning by small steps, explained in easy English with a hands-on page.

content.text: Many people think AI needs advanced maths and stop before they start. The truth is kinder. To use and build with AI tools you need only a handful of ideas, and each one can be explained with a picture or a small example. In this lesson you will learn five of them: vectors, similarity, averages and spread, probability, and learning by taking small steps downhill. At the end you will build a page in the lab where you can play with each idea and see the numbers change.

If maths felt hard at school, relax. We use no hard formulas. Every formula in this lesson is only a few symbols, and the code in the lab does all the calculation for you. What matters is the meaning behind the numbers.
Idea 1: a vector is a list of numbers

A **vector** is just a list of numbers in a fixed order. A person’s profile can be a vector: [years of experience, number of skills, expected salary]. Someone with 3 years, 5 skills and a 40 thousand salary is the vector [3, 5, 40]. Once things are lists of numbers, a computer can compare, add and measure them.

This idea is everywhere in AI. When a model reads a word or a sentence, it first turns it into a long vector, sometimes with thousands of numbers. We call that an **embedding**, and you will meet it again in later courses. For now, remember this: AI does not see words or pictures. It sees lists of numbers.
Idea 2: similarity, or how close are two vectors?

If two things are lists of numbers, we can ask how similar they are. One popular answer is **cosine similarity**. Imagine each vector as an arrow starting from the same point. If two arrows point in nearly the same direction, the things are similar. If they point in completely different directions, they are not. Cosine similarity gives a number from -1 to 1. A value close to 1 means the arrows point the same way. A value near 0 means they are unrelated. A value close to -1 means they point in opposite ways.

Example: take A = [1, 2, 3] and B = [2, 4, 6]. B is just A doubled, so the arrows point in exactly the same direction and the similarity is 1. Now take A = [1, 0] and B = [0, 1]. They point at right angles, and the similarity is 0. Notice that cosine similarity ignores length and cares only about direction. That is useful for text, because a long document and a short document about the same topic should still count as similar.

The calculation uses two small helpers. The **dot product** multiplies the numbers in the same positions and adds the results: for [1, 2, 3] and [2, 4, 6] it is 1×2 + 2×4 + 3×6 = 28. The **norm** is the length of an arrow: the square root of the vector’s dot product with itself. Cosine similarity is the dot product divided by the two lengths multiplied together.
Idea 3: averages and spread

The **mean** is the average: add the numbers and divide by how many there are. If five candidates ask for 20, 22, 25, 24 and 60 thousand, the mean is 30.2 thousand. But look: four of the five asked for 25 or less. One large number pulled the average up. This is why you should always check the **spread** as well as the mean.

The **standard deviation** measures spread. A small value means the numbers are close together. A large value means they are scattered. In AI we use the mean and spread constantly: to check whether data looks normal, to scale numbers so that big ones do not dominate, and to measure how stable a result is. If a model’s accuracy is 90 percent on one test and 70 percent on another, a high spread tells you that you cannot trust a single number.
Idea 4: probability and softmax

**Probability** is a number between 0 and 1 that tells you how likely something is. 0 means it never happens, 1 means it always does, and 0.25 means one time in four. The probabilities of all possible outcomes must add up to 1.

Models usually do not start with probabilities. They start with raw **scores**, which can be any number, positive or negative. To turn scores into probabilities we use a function called **softmax**. It makes every score positive (by using the exponential), then divides each by the total so that everything adds up to 1. A higher score always gets a higher probability, and the gap grows quickly. With the scores [2, 1, 0] the probabilities are about 0.66, 0.24 and 0.09.

Softmax matters because language models choose the next word with it. For every possible next token, the model produces a score, and softmax turns the scores into probabilities. Lesson 6 shows how settings like temperature change this step.
Idea 5: learning is walking downhill

How does a model learn? Picture yourself standing on a hill in thick fog. You cannot see the valley, but you can feel the slope under your feet. A simple plan works: take a small step in the direction that goes downhill, feel the slope again, and repeat. After many steps you reach the bottom.

In machine learning, the “height” of the hill is the **error**, how wrong the model is. The “position” is the model’s set of numbers, called **weights** or **parameters**. The **gradient** is the slope: it tells the model which way to change each weight to reduce the error. The **learning rate** is the size of your step. If the steps are too small, learning takes forever. If they are too big, you jump over the valley and may never settle. Training a large language model is this same idea repeated billions of times, with billions of weights.

Install Node.js 20 or newer, unzip the solution zip for the lesson, run npm install, then npm start and open http://localhost:4200. The zip for each lesson contains the whole lab up to that lesson, so you can start from any lesson. The models in these exercises are tiny teaching models. They show how the ideas work, but they are not real language models.
Your task: a playground for the five ideas
Build a page called Maths that lets you play with each idea. You will write four small functions and one page that uses them.
**What you will build**

items: Functions for the dot product, the norm and cosine similarity, plus the mean and the standard deviation.
A softmax function that turns any list of scores into probabilities that add up to 1.
A gradient step function that moves a number downhill on a simple curve, so you can watch it converge.
An Angular page with four small cards: vectors, averages, softmax and learning.

content.text: **Steps**

items: Create src/app/lib/math.ts. Write parseVector, which turns a text like “1, 2, 3” into [1, 2, 3] and ignores anything that is not a number.
Write dot, norm and cosine. In cosine, return 0 when either vector has length 0 so that you never divide by zero.
Write mean and stdDev. For the standard deviation, take the average of the squared distances from the mean, then the square root.
Write softmax. Subtract the largest score from every score first. This does not change the result, but it keeps the exponentials from becoming huge numbers.
Write gradientSteps(start, target, rate, steps) for the curve y = (x - target)². The slope at x is 2 × (x - target). Move x by -rate × slope at every step and keep the path.
Build src/app/pages/vectors.ts with inputs for two vectors, a list of numbers, a list of scores, and sliders for the target and the step size. Show the results and the path of the learning steps.

content.text: **Hints**

items: For two vectors of different length, treat missing numbers as 0.
Try the scores [2, 1, 0] and then [20, 10, 0]. Watch how the biggest score takes almost everything.
Try a step size of 0.1, then 0.9, then 1.1. At 1.1 the walk jumps further away each time. This is called divergence.
Add an extreme number such as 500 to your list of salaries and watch the mean move more than the middle value does.

What you learned

items: A vector is a list of numbers. AI turns words, pictures and people into vectors.
Cosine similarity measures how close the direction of two vectors is, from -1 to 1.
The mean is the average; the standard deviation shows how scattered the numbers are. Always look at both.
Softmax turns raw scores into probabilities that add up to 1.
Learning means taking small steps downhill on an error curve. The learning rate is the step size.

content.text: In the next lesson you will use these ideas to train a model that learns from labelled examples, and you will see how it can fail by memorising instead of learning.

faqs.q: Do I need to know calculus to understand AI?
faqs.a: To build apps with AI tools, no. Calculus explains how the slope (gradient) is calculated, but the libraries do that for you. The idea of taking small steps downhill is enough to start.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a vector and an embedding?
faqs.a: A vector is any list of numbers. An embedding is a vector produced by a model to represent the meaning of a word, a sentence or an image, so that similar things get similar vectors.

faqs.q: Why does softmax subtract the largest score first?
faqs.a: It keeps the numbers small and stable. Without it, a score of 1000 would make the exponential too large for a computer to handle. The final probabilities are the same either way.

faqs.q: What is a good learning rate?
faqs.a: There is no single answer. Too small is slow and too large is unstable. People try a few values, watch the error, and pick one where the error goes down smoothly. Many tools adjust the rate automatically.

lessons.title: Machine Learning Basics
lessons.description: Learn supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning, why we split data into training and test sets, what overfitting is, and build a k-nearest-neighbours classifier.

content.text: Machine learning, or ML, is the part of AI where a program learns from data instead of following rules written by a person. You met the idea in lesson 1. In this lesson we go one level deeper: the main types of learning, the basic steps of a machine learning project, and the most important warning in the whole field, overfitting. You will build a small classifier that decides whether a candidate should be shortlisted, and you will watch it succeed and fail in a way that mirrors real projects.
Three ways a machine can learn

**Supervised learning** is learning from labelled examples. Each example comes with the right answer: this resume was shortlisted, this one was not; this email is spam, this one is not. The model learns to predict the label for new examples. Most business uses of ML are supervised: price prediction, spam filters, document classification, and so on.

**Unsupervised learning** has no labels. You give the model data and ask it to find structure. A typical use is clustering: grouping customers or job postings into sets of similar items, without anyone saying what the groups should be. Another is finding unusual items that do not fit any group.

**Reinforcement learning** learns by trying things and receiving rewards or penalties. A game-playing program wins or loses and adjusts. This method is also used to refine chat assistants: people rate answers, and the model is nudged towards answers that people prefer.

Large language models use a mix. Their first stage, predicting the next word in huge amounts of text, is often called self-supervised: the text itself supplies the answers, so no one has to label anything. You will learn more about this in lessons 5 and 6.
The steps of a supervised project

items: **Collect data.** Gather examples with correct labels. This is usually the hardest and most expensive step.
**Clean and prepare.** Fix errors, remove duplicates, turn text into numbers, and scale the numbers.
**Split.** Keep some examples hidden for testing. More on this below.
**Train.** Let the model learn from the training part.
**Evaluate.** Check the model on the test part, which it has never seen.
**Use and watch.** Put the model to work and keep checking it, because the real world changes.

content.text: Train and test: the most important habit

Imagine a student who gets the exam questions in advance and memorises the answers. Their exam score will be perfect, but it tells you nothing about what they understand. Machine learning has the same problem. If you test a model on the same examples it learned from, the score is meaningless.

So we split the data. The larger part is the **training set**, used for learning. The smaller part, often 20 to 30 percent, is the **test set**. The model never sees it while learning. The score on the test set is an honest estimate of how the model will do on new data.
Overfitting and underfitting

**Overfitting** happens when a model learns the training examples too closely, including their accidents and noise, and then does poorly on new data. The sign is a big gap: very high accuracy on the training set and much lower accuracy on the test set. **Underfitting** is the opposite: the model is too simple to catch the real pattern, and it does poorly on both sets.

Think about a resume screening model trained on only 30 past hires. If three of the shortlisted people happened to have the same hobby, a model that fits too closely might decide the hobby matters. On new candidates it would be wrong in odd ways. More data, simpler models and honest testing are the usual cures.
Measuring the result: accuracy, precision and recall

The simplest measure is **accuracy**: the share of predictions that are correct. But accuracy can mislead. If only 5 percent of candidates are a good match, a lazy model that says “no” every time is 95 percent accurate and totally useless. So we look at a table called the **confusion matrix**, which counts four outcomes: true positives (said yes, correctly), false positives (said yes, wrongly), true negatives (said no, correctly) and false negatives (said no, wrongly).

items: **Precision** answers: of everyone the model said yes to, how many were really yes? It matters when a false alarm is costly.
**Recall** answers: of everyone who was really yes, how many did the model find? It matters when missing a good case is costly.

content.text: In a hiring tool, low recall means good candidates are rejected without anyone noticing. That is why human review of rejected cases matters.
A simple model: k nearest neighbours

The model in this lesson is **k-nearest neighbours**, or k-NN. It is one of the simplest ML methods. To judge a new candidate, find the k training examples that are closest to them (using a distance, like in lesson 2), and let those neighbours vote. If most of the neighbours were shortlisted, predict “shortlisted”. The number k is a setting you choose. With k = 1 the model copies its single nearest neighbour, which follows every accident in the data and overfits easily. With a very large k the model averages too much and underfits. A medium k often works best, and the test set helps you find it.

Install Node.js 20 or newer, unzip the solution zip for the lesson, run npm install, then npm start and open http://localhost:4200. The zip for each lesson contains the whole lab up to that lesson, so you can start from any lesson. The models in these exercises are tiny teaching models. They show how the ideas work, but they are not real language models.
Your task: a shortlisting classifier

You will build a page that generates a fake set of candidates, splits them into training and test sets, classifies with k-NN, and shows accuracy, precision, recall and the confusion matrix. You will use sliders for k, the test share and the amount of noise.
**What you will build**

items: A seeded random number generator, so that the same seed always gives the same data. This makes experiments repeatable.
A function makeData that creates candidates with years of experience and a skills score. A candidate is shortlisted when a mix of the two is high, but noise flips some labels.
A split function that shuffles and divides the data.
A predict function for k-NN and an evaluate function that returns the confusion matrix, accuracy, precision and recall.
A page with sliders and results for the training and the test data.

Write lib/knn.ts. In makeData, create the requested number of people with random years (0 to 15) and skills (0 to 10). Decide the label from a simple formula, then flip it with a probability equal to the noise setting.
Write split(data, testShare, seed) that shuffles a copy and returns the train and test arrays.
Write predict(train, who, k): measure the distance to every training example, sort, take the k nearest and vote.
Write evaluate(train, test, k) that counts tp, fp, tn and fn and calculates accuracy, precision and recall. Avoid dividing by zero.
Build the page. Show the accuracy on the training data and on the test data side by side.

content.text: **Hints**

items: When you test on the training data with k = 1, accuracy is 100 percent or very close to it, because each point’s nearest neighbour is itself. This is a good way to see why a separate test set matters.
Set the noise to a high value. The test accuracy falls, and the gap between train and test grows with small k.
Use an odd k to avoid tied votes.
Change only one slider at a time, so you can see the cause of each change.

content.text: **You know it works when** the training accuracy with k = 1 is 100 percent (or very close) while the test accuracy is clearly lower, a medium k closes the gap between training and test scores (the test score is not always higher, since small test sets are noisy), and changing the seed gives a different but similar picture.

What you learned

items: Supervised learning uses labelled examples, unsupervised learning finds structure without labels, and reinforcement learning uses rewards.

faqs.q: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?
faqs.a: Supervised learning uses examples with correct answers (labels) and learns to predict them. Unsupervised learning has no labels and looks for structure, such as groups of similar items.

faqs.q: How much data do I need for machine learning?
faqs.a: It depends on the task. Simple patterns with few features can work with hundreds of examples. Complex tasks like language need millions. More important than the amount is that the data is correct and similar to what the model will meet in real use.

faqs.q: How can I tell that a model is overfitting?
faqs.a: Compare the score on the training data with the score on the test data. A high training score and a much lower test score is the classic sign.

faqs.q: Is a high accuracy always good?
faqs.a: No. If one class is rare, a model that always predicts the common class has high accuracy and no value. Check precision, recall and the confusion matrix.

lessons.title: Deep Learning and Transformers
lessons.description: Understand neural networks, layers and training, learn the idea of attention and the transformer, and train a small neural network in your browser.

content.text: Deep learning is the technology behind modern image recognition, speech recognition and large language models. The name sounds mysterious, but the core idea is small. A neural network is a chain of simple calculations, repeated in layers, with numbers that are adjusted by learning. In this lesson you will learn what a neuron is, why layers matter, how training works, and what a transformer is. Then you will train a real neural network in your browser and watch it learn a problem that a simple model cannot solve.
A neuron is a small calculator

An artificial **neuron** does three things. It takes several input numbers. It multiplies each input by a **weight** (a number that says how important that input is) and adds the results together with one extra number called the **bias**. Then it passes the total through an **activation function**, a small curve that squeezes the result into a useful range. A common choice is the sigmoid, which turns any number into a value between 0 and 1.

Example: a neuron that guesses whether a candidate is a good match takes two inputs, years of experience and number of relevant skills. If its weights are 0.4 and 0.8, a person with 3 years and 5 skills gives 0.4×3 + 0.8×5 = 5.2, plus a bias. A large positive total gives an output near 1, which we read as “likely a match”.
Why we need layers

One neuron can only draw a straight line between two groups. Some problems cannot be split by a straight line. The classic example is **XOR**, short for “exclusive or”: the answer is 1 when exactly one of two inputs is 1, but 0 when both are 0 or both are 1. In words: “one or the other, but not both”. If you plot the four cases, no single straight line puts the two 1 answers on one side and the two 0 answers on the other.

The fix is to add a **hidden layer**: a middle row of neurons between the inputs and the output. Each hidden neuron makes its own simple judgement. The output neuron then combines their judgements. Together they can draw curves and corners that one neuron cannot. A network with many hidden layers is called a **deep** network, which is where the name deep learning comes from. Each layer learns something a bit more abstract than the layer before: in an image model, the first layers find edges, the next find shapes, and the later ones find faces or objects.
How a network trains
A new network starts with random weights, so its answers are nonsense. Training repeats four steps many times:

items: **Forward pass.** Give the network an example and let it calculate an answer.
**Compare.** Measure the error between its answer and the right answer.
**Backward pass.** Use a method called **backpropagation** to work out how much each weight contributed to the error. This is the gradient from lesson 2, found for every weight.
**Update.** Move each weight a small step in the direction that reduces the error, using the learning rate.

content.text: One full pass over all training examples is called an **epoch**. After many epochs, the error falls and the network’s answers get close to the targets. You will see this in the lab: the error bars get shorter as training goes on.
Neural networks need a lot of calculation, which is why graphics processors (GPUs) became important. They do thousands of small multiplications at the same time.
From networks to transformers

Before 2017, most language models read text one word at a time, in order, and kept a small memory of what came before. They were slow to train and forgot the start of long sentences. In 2017 researchers at Google published a paper called “Attention Is All You Need” that introduced the **transformer**, the design behind almost every large language model today.

The key idea is **attention**. When the model processes a word, attention lets it look at all the other words in the text and decide which ones matter for understanding this one. Take the sentence: “The candidate sent the resume to the manager because **she** liked the profile.” To understand “she”, the model must connect it to the right person. Attention gives each word a way to ask, “Which other words should I pay attention to?” and to collect information from them, weighted by importance.

Attention has two big advantages. It can connect words that are far apart, so long sentences are not forgotten. And all the words can be processed at the same time instead of one by one, which fits GPUs very well and made it possible to train on enormous amounts of text. A transformer stacks many layers of attention, each followed by a small neural network. Lesson 7 explains this stack in more detail.

A final point to remember: a transformer does not store facts in a database. Its knowledge is spread across billions of weights, adjusted during training. That is why it can write fluent text and also why it can be wrong without warning.

faqs.q: What is the difference between deep learning and machine learning?
faqs.a: Deep learning is a kind of machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. Other machine learning methods, such as k-NN or decision trees, are not deep learning.

faqs.q: What does attention do in a transformer?
faqs.a: Attention lets the model compare each word with every other word in the text and decide which ones are most useful for understanding it. This helps it handle long sentences and connect words that are far apart.

faqs.q: Why do neural networks need GPUs?
faqs.a: Training means a huge number of multiplications that can run at the same time. GPUs are built to do many such calculations in parallel, so they are much faster than ordinary processors for this work.

faqs.q: Can a neural network explain its decisions?
faqs.a: Not easily. The answer comes from many weights working together, so there is no single rule to point to. Researchers work on explanation methods, but for important decisions a human check is still needed.

lessons.title: Introduction to Generative AI
lessons.description: Learn what generative AI is, how it differs from predictive AI, what it can create and where it fails, and build a tiny text generator that shows the core idea.

content.text: Until a few years ago, most AI products were built to judge or predict: is this email spam, will this customer leave, which job fits this resume best. Today, many AI products are built to create: they write an email, draw a picture, compose a tune, or write computer code. This second kind is called **generative AI**. In this lesson you will learn what makes it different, what it can make, how the simplest possible text generator works, and where generative AI goes wrong. You will build that simplest generator yourself, in a few lines of code, and see why it is a good first picture of how a large language model behaves.
Predictive AI and generative AI

**Predictive AI**, sometimes called discriminative AI, looks at an input and chooses from a small set of answers. A spam filter says “spam” or “not spam”. A resume screener gives a score from 0 to 100. The output is a label or a number.

**Generative AI** produces something new that was not in the input: a paragraph, an image, a song, a piece of code. The output is open-ended. There is no short list of correct answers. If you ask a generative model for “a cover letter for a warehouse job”, there are millions of acceptable letters.

Underneath, both kinds learn patterns from data. A generative model learns the patterns of how things look: how sentences are built, how pictures are arranged. Then it uses those patterns to produce new examples that look similar to what it learned from. It does not copy and paste a stored example. It produces new output one small piece at a time.
What generative AI can create

items: **Text.** Emails, summaries, translations, stories, explanations and answers. This is where large language models (LLMs) work.
**Code.** Programs, tests, and fixes for bugs, often from a plain-English description.
**Images.** Pictures from a written description, or edits to an existing photo.
**Audio and music.** Speech in a chosen voice, sound effects, songs.
**Video.** Short clips from a description or a still image.
**Structured data.** Tables, JSON and database queries. You will use this in the prompt engineering lessons.

content.text: This course focuses on text, because text models are the base of most business tools: chat assistants, resume writers, search with answers, and support bots.
The core idea: predict the next piece

A language model has one basic skill. Given some text, it estimates which piece of text is likely to come next. A **piece** is usually a word or part of a word, called a token (lesson 6 explains tokens). Write “Thank you for your” and the model finds that “time”, “help” and “application” are likely, while “banana” is not. It picks one of them, adds it to the text, and repeats. That loop, repeated hundreds of times, produces a whole paragraph.

It may sound too simple to produce useful answers, but there is a catch: to predict the next word well across all kinds of text, the model must learn a lot about grammar, facts, style and even some reasoning. Predicting the next word in a maths textbook rewards knowing some maths. Predicting the next word in a polite email rewards knowing how polite emails sound.

The simplest version of this idea needs no neural network at all. It is called a **Markov chain**. You look at the last one or two words, find every place in your training text where those words appeared, and note which word came next each time. To generate, you pick one of those next words at random, add it, shift forward by one word, and repeat. Words that followed more often are picked more often.

Example: suppose the training text contains “the manager reviews the resume” and “the manager calls the candidate”. After the words “the manager” the possible next words are “reviews” and “calls”. The chain picks one. If it picks “calls”, then looks at “manager calls”, the next word can only be “the”, and so on. The output can combine pieces in ways that never appeared as a whole in the training text.
Why a Markov chain is not enough

Your tiny generator will sound a little like the text it was trained on, but it has no real idea of meaning. It sees only the last one or two words. With a short memory it writes nonsense that drifts away from any topic. With a long memory (many words) it simply copies whole pieces of the original, because there is only one thing that ever followed those words. You will measure this in the exercise: a number that shows what share of the output is copied from the source.

A large language model solves this by looking at thousands of previous words at once, by using attention (lesson 4) and by learning from a vast amount of text. Instead of counting exact word matches, it learns a smooth sense of similarity, so it can handle sentences it has never seen. But the loop is the same: look at the text so far, estimate the likely next token, pick one, repeat.
Where generative AI fails
Because the model produces what is likely, not what is true, it has a few typical weaknesses. Learn them now, because later lessons show how to reduce each one.

items: **Hallucination.** The model states something false in a confident voice. A made-up quotation, a wrong date, a fake web address. It happens because a fluent guess looks the same as a fact from the model’s point of view.
**Out-of-date knowledge.** The model learned from text up to a certain date and knows nothing after it, unless you give it new information.
**Bias.** The training text came from people, so the model can repeat stereotypes found there.
**Inconsistency.** Ask the same question twice and you may get two different answers, because the choice of the next token has some randomness.
**Prompt sensitivity.** Small changes to the wording of a request can change the quality of the answer. This is why prompt engineering exists.

content.text: None of this means generative AI is useless. It means you should use it the way you would use a quick, well-read, over-confident assistant: great for drafts, ideas and summaries, but needing a check before important facts go out under your name.
Using generative AI responsibly

Three simple habits help. First, **check facts** that matter: numbers, names, dates, links and anything legal or medical. Second, **protect private data**: do not paste passwords, ID numbers or other people’s personal details into a tool unless you know how it stores them. Third, **be honest** about where text came from when it matters, for example in school or in a professional setting. A resume written with AI help is fine, but every claim in it must still be true.

faqs.q: What is the difference between generative AI and a chatbot?
faqs.a: Generative AI is the technology that creates new content. A chatbot is one application that uses it, wrapped in a chat window. Many chatbots use a large language model to generate their replies.

faqs.q: Does generative AI copy existing text?
faqs.a: It does not look up and paste stored text, but it can reproduce passages that appeared many times in its training data. It generates output one token at a time based on learned patterns.

faqs.q: Why does generative AI sometimes say false things?
faqs.a: It produces text that is likely given the patterns it learned, and it has no built-in way to check facts. A fluent false sentence can be as likely as a true one, so the model may write it with confidence.

faqs.q: Is a Markov chain a real language model?
faqs.a: Yes, it is the oldest and simplest type of statistical language model. Modern models are far larger and use neural networks and attention, but they share the idea of predicting the next piece of text.

lessons.title: How Large Language Models Work
lessons.description: Understand tokens, the context window, training and sampling settings like temperature, top-k and top-p, with a hands-on page that shows how the next word is chosen.

content.text: A large language model, or LLM, is a very big neural network trained on a very large amount of text to predict the next token. You met that idea in the last lesson. In this lesson we open the box a little. You will learn what a token is, what the context window limits, how the model is trained in stages, and how settings such as temperature change the way the model picks its next word. By the end you will be able to explain why the same question can give different answers, and you will have a page where you can see the effect of every setting.
Tokens: the pieces a model reads

A model does not read letters or whole words. It reads **tokens**. A token is a piece of text, often a common word, part of a longer word, or a bit of punctuation. A simple word such as “job” is usually one token. A rare word such as “unemployability” may be split into several pieces. The splitting method is learned from data so that common pieces get their own token, which keeps text short.

As a rough guide for English, one token is about four characters, or three quarters of a word. So 100 words are around 130 tokens. Other languages often need more tokens for the same meaning, because the tokenizer saw less text in them. Numbers, code and unusual names can use many tokens too.

Tokens matter for three reasons. They decide the **cost**, because most AI services charge by the token for input and output. They decide the **limit**, because a model can only handle a fixed number of tokens at once. And they explain some odd behaviour: a model that sees “strawberry” as a few pieces rather than ten letters can find it hard to count letters.
The context window

The **context window** is the maximum number of tokens the model can look at in one go. It includes everything: your instructions, earlier messages in the chat, any documents you pasted, and the answer being written. Think of it as the model’s desk. Anything on the desk can be used. Anything that does not fit is simply not there.

Windows have grown from a few thousand tokens to hundreds of thousands, and some models handle more than a million. But a bigger window is not magic. Longer input costs more and runs slower. Models can also pay less attention to the middle of very long text. A good habit is to put only what the model needs into the window, and to place the most important instructions clearly, near the start or the end.

The model has no memory between separate conversations unless the application stores and re-sends earlier messages. When a chat seems to “remember” you, the app is putting the earlier text back into the context window each time.
How a model is trained

items: **Pre-training.** The model reads a huge collection of text (books, websites, code, articles) and learns to predict the next token. It makes a guess, compares it with the real next token, and adjusts its weights, billions of times. This is the most expensive stage and builds the broad knowledge and language skill.

**Instruction tuning.** The pre-trained model only continues text. It is then trained on examples of questions with good answers, so that it learns to follow instructions and to behave like an assistant.

**Preference training.** People compare answers and say which one is better. The model is adjusted towards answers people prefer: more helpful, more honest, and less harmful. Methods in this stage include reinforcement learning from human feedback.

content.text: After training, the weights are fixed. When you use the model, it does not learn from your chat. This is why a model cannot know about last week’s news, unless a tool provides it.
Choosing the next token

At each step the model produces one raw score for every token in its vocabulary, which can have 100 thousand entries or more. Softmax (lesson 2) turns the scores into probabilities. Then the program must pick one token. How it picks is controlled by a few settings.

**Greedy choice** always takes the most likely token. The output is steady and repeatable but can be dull and repetitive. **Sampling** picks randomly in proportion to the probabilities, so a token with 20 percent chance is chosen about one time in five. This gives variety.

items: **Temperature** reshapes the probabilities before sampling. The scores are divided by the temperature. A low temperature, such as 0.2, makes the favourite token dominate, so answers are focused and consistent. A high temperature, such as 1.5, flattens the probabilities, so unlikely tokens get a real chance and answers become more varied and sometimes strange. Temperature 0 means always the top token.
**Top-k** keeps only the k most likely tokens and drops the rest. With top-k = 3 the model chooses among the three best candidates.

**Top-p**, also called nucleus sampling, keeps the smallest group of top tokens whose probabilities add up to p. With top-p = 0.9 it keeps just enough tokens to cover 90 percent of the probability. The group is small when the model is sure and large when it is not.

content.text: After top-k or top-p removes some tokens, the remaining probabilities are scaled up to add to 1 again, and one token is sampled. For facts, extraction and code, use a low temperature. For brainstorming and creative writing, a medium or higher temperature helps. Not every model or service lets you set all of these, so read the documentation of the one you use.

Even at a low temperature, the same prompt may not give exactly the same answer every time, because of small differences in how the calculations run. If you need exact repeatability, test your prompt many times and check the results, rather than trusting one run.
Why the model sounds so sure

The model produces a fluent answer whether or not it knows the facts, because fluency is exactly what it was trained for. Its internal probabilities are not a reliable measure of truth. So treat confident wording as style, not as proof. You can reduce the risk by giving the model the source text to work from, asking it to say when it does not know, and checking claims that matter.

Write sampleMany(probs, times, seed): for each draw, take a random number and subtract probabilities from a random number until it drops to zero or below to pick an index. Count how often each index is chosen.
Write estimateTokens(text): words × 1.3, and characters ÷ 4. Show both, since they are only guesses.

items: A model reads tokens, about four characters or three quarters of a word each in English, and tokens decide cost and limits.

faqs.q: What is a token in an LLM?
faqs.a: A token is a small piece of text that the model reads and writes: a short word, part of a longer word, or punctuation. In English one token is about four characters or three quarters of a word.

faqs.q: What does temperature do?
faqs.a: Temperature controls randomness in choosing the next token. A low value makes the model pick the most likely tokens and give steady answers. A high value gives more varied and sometimes less accurate answers.

faqs.q: Does the model learn from my conversation?
faqs.a: Not in the moment. The weights are fixed after training. Apps may seem to remember by sending earlier messages back into the context window, and some providers may use data for future training under their own policies, so check the privacy settings.

faqs.q: Should I use top-k and top-p together?
faqs.a: You can, but changing one of them is usually enough. Many guides suggest adjusting either temperature or top-p, not both at once, so that you can see the effect of each change.

lessons.description: Learn the parts of a transformer, parameters, the cache and mixture of experts, and how quantization, batching and smaller models cut memory, cost and delay. Includes a model size calculator.

content.text: In lesson 4 you met the transformer. In this lesson you will look at its parts in a little more detail, and then at a very practical question: what does it take to run a model? A model with billions of parameters needs memory, and it needs to read that memory for every token it writes. Understanding this explains why some models run on a phone and others need a data centre, why long chats cost more, and why people talk about quantization, caching and small models. At the end you will build a calculator that estimates whether a model fits on a device and how fast it can run.
The parts of a transformer
A modern language model is a stack of identical **blocks**. The number of blocks, often between 20 and 100 or more, is the model’s depth. Each block has two main parts.

items: **Self-attention.** Every token looks at the other tokens before it and collects the information it needs, weighted by importance. Many attention “heads” run side by side, and each can focus on a different kind of relation: grammar, names, topic, position.
**A feed-forward network.** A small neural network applied to each token on its own. Much of the model’s stored knowledge is thought to sit here.

content.text: Around those parts are a few helpers. The first step turns each token into a vector, the **embedding**, and adds information about its **position**, because attention alone does not know which word came first. **Normalisation** layers keep the numbers in a healthy range. **Residual connections** add each block’s input back to its output, which lets very deep networks train without losing the signal. At the top, a final layer turns the last vector into one score for every token in the vocabulary, and softmax produces the probabilities you saw in lesson 6.
What are parameters?

The **parameters** of a model are its weights: all the numbers adjusted during training. When you read “a 7 billion parameter model”, it means 7,000,000,000 numbers. More parameters usually give more capacity to store knowledge and skill, but they also need more memory and more calculation. Size is not everything: a smaller model trained on better data, for longer, can beat a bigger one.

Parameters are not the same as the context window or the amount of training text. Parameters are the model’s size. The context window is how much it can read at once. The training data is what it learned from.
How much memory does a model need?
Each parameter is a number that must be stored, and the space it takes depends on its **precision**. The common choices are:

items: **32-bit floating point (fp32)** takes 4 bytes per parameter. It is precise and was used for training in the past.
**16-bit floating point (fp16 or bf16)** takes 2 bytes. It is the usual choice for serving models.
**8-bit integer (int8)** takes 1 byte.
**4-bit integer (int4)** takes half a byte.

content.text: The memory for the weights is simply the number of parameters multiplied by the bytes per parameter. A 7 billion parameter model in 16-bit takes 7 billion × 2 bytes = 14 gigabytes. In 4-bit it takes about 3.5 gigabytes. You also need extra space for working data. A rough rule is to add about 20 percent, and more for long conversations.
Quantization: smaller numbers, smaller model

**Quantization** means storing the weights with fewer bits. It is like saving a photo at lower quality: the file is much smaller, and if you do it with care you hardly see the difference. Going from 16-bit to 8-bit halves the memory, and to 4-bit cuts it to a quarter. The model also runs faster, as we will see next. The cost is a small loss of quality, which grows as you use fewer bits. Many everyday tasks are fine at 8-bit or even 4-bit, but you should test your own task, especially for maths, code and non-English languages.
Why speed depends on memory

When a model writes text it produces one token at a time. For each token it needs to use all of its weights, so the chip must read the whole model from memory again and again. For this reason, the writing speed is usually limited by **memory bandwidth**, how many gigabytes per second the chip can read, and not by how fast it can multiply.

A rough upper limit is: tokens per second ≈ memory bandwidth ÷ size of the weights. With a model of 14 GB and a chip that reads 900 GB per second, the limit is about 64 tokens per second. Quantize the same model to 4-bit (3.5 GB) and the limit rises to about 257. These are only estimates. Real speed depends on the software, how many requests are handled together, and the hardware. But the estimate shows an important truth: smaller weights mean both less memory and more speed.
The cache: why long chats get expensive

When a model has already processed your earlier tokens, it does not want to redo the work for each new token. It keeps the intermediate results of attention for all earlier tokens, called the **KV cache** (keys and values). This saves a lot of calculation but uses memory that grows with the length of the conversation and with the number of users served at once. That is one reason why very long contexts are slow and costly, and why services may charge differently for cached and uncached input.
More ways to make models cheaper and faster

items: **Batching.** Serve many users at the same time, so that one read of the weights helps many requests.
**Smaller models and distillation.** Train a small “student” model to copy the behaviour of a big “teacher” model. You get much of the quality at a fraction of the cost.

**Mixture of experts (MoE).** The model contains many specialist sub-networks, and for each token only a few are used. The model has many parameters in total but uses only part of them per token, which saves calculation.
**Efficient attention methods.** Software tricks that compute attention faster and with less memory.
**Caching prompts and answers.** If many requests start with the same long instructions, or ask the same question, reuse the earlier work or answer.

content.text: Choosing a model is a trade-off between quality, speed, cost and privacy. A small model on your own device is private and free per use but less capable. A large hosted model is more capable but costs money per token and sends your data to a provider. A good engineer picks the smallest model that does the job well, and tests that claim.

faqs.q: What does 7B mean in a model name?
faqs.a: It means about 7 billion parameters, the number of weights in the model. Larger numbers usually mean more capability but also more memory and cost.

faqs.q: Does quantization make a model worse?
faqs.a: Slightly, and the loss grows as you use fewer bits. At 8-bit the change is often tiny. At 4-bit it is usually acceptable for many tasks. Always test your own task to be sure.

faqs.q: Why is a long chat slower and more expensive?
faqs.a: The model must keep and attend to the cache of every earlier token. That uses more memory and more calculation, and many services charge for all input tokens each time.

faqs.q: Is a bigger model always better?
faqs.a: No. A smaller model with better training data can do well on a specific task, and it is cheaper and faster. Choose the smallest model that meets your quality needs after testing.

lessons.title: Prompt Engineering Basics
lessons.description: Learn how to write clear prompts with a role, task, context, rules, examples and an output format, and build a prompt builder with a checker.

content.text: A **prompt** is the text you give a model. **Prompt engineering** is the skill of writing prompts so that the model gives answers that are useful, correct and in the shape you need. It sounds fancy, but at its heart it is clear writing. If you can explain a job to a new colleague so that they do it well the first time, you can write good prompts. In this lesson you will learn a simple structure that works for most tasks, see a weak prompt turn into a strong one, and build a prompt builder in the lab that assembles the parts and warns you about common gaps.
Why prompts matter

A model cannot read your mind. It sees only the text you send. If your request is vague, the model fills the gaps with the most likely guess, which may not be what you want. Ask for “a good resume summary” and you will get a generic summary that could be about anybody. Ask for “a two-sentence resume summary for a warehouse supervisor with five years of experience who reduced picking errors by 20 percent, in simple English, with no buzzwords” and the result will fit.
Prompting is not a trick to fool the model. It is a way to remove guessing. Every detail you add is one less thing the model must invent.
The six parts of a good prompt
Most strong prompts contain some or all of these six parts. You do not need all of them every time. Use the ones that matter for the task.

items: **Role.** Who the model should act as. “You are a careful career coach for factory and warehouse workers.” A role sets the tone and the level of detail.
**Task.** What exactly to do, starting with a verb. “Rewrite the resume bullet below so that it starts with an action verb and shows a result.”

**Context.** The material to work on, and any background the model needs: the resume text, the job description, the customer email. Put it between clear markers, such as <context> tags, so the model can tell data from instructions.
**Rules.** The limits: “Do not invent numbers.” “Use simple English.” “Keep it under 25 words.” Rules prevent the most common problems before they happen.

**Examples.** One to three pairs of input and output that show the style you want. Examples are often the strongest way to communicate a format. Use different examples so that the model does not copy a single one too closely.
**Output format.** How the answer should look: bullets, a table, a number of sentences, or JSON. If a program will read the answer, the format must be exact (lesson 10).

content.text: A weak prompt and a strong prompt
Weak prompt:
Improve this: Responsible for stock and loading at the warehouse
The model must guess what “improve” means, who the reader is, how long the result should be, and whether it may add facts. It may add invented numbers or write a long paragraph.
Strong prompt:

You are a careful career coach for factory and warehouse workers.

Task: Rewrite the resume bullet below so it starts with an action verb and shows a result.

Context:
<context>
Responsible for stock and loading at the warehouse
</context>

Rules:
- Do not invent numbers.
- Use simple English.

Examples:
<example n="1">
Input: Did customer calls
Output: Handled 40 customer calls a day and solved 90% of issues on the first call
</example>

Output format: One bullet under 25 words. No extra text.

This takes a minute longer to write. But the result is much more predictable, and when it is not right you can see which part to fix. Notice one more detail: the rule “do not invent numbers” sits right next to an example that contains numbers. If the example contains numbers, the model may copy that style and invent some. This kind of clash between rules and examples is a common cause of errors, so read your own prompt the way the model will.
Habits that make prompts better

items: **Be specific.** Replace words like “good”, “nice”, “some” and “etc” with something you can measure: “three bullets, each under 20 words”.
**Say what to do, not only what to avoid.** “Write in plain sentences” works better than “don’t be fancy”.
**Give the reader.** “Explain it for a factory worker who has never used a computer” changes the whole answer.
**Separate instructions from data.** Use tags or clear markers around pasted text. This also protects you from text that tries to give the model new instructions (lesson 11).
**Allow “I don’t know”.** Add “If the answer is not in the text, say so.” This reduces made-up answers.
**Ask for the steps when the task is complex.** For maths or multi-step problems, ask the model to work through the steps before giving the answer. Lesson 9 covers this.
**Iterate.** Your first prompt is a draft. Run it on several real inputs, find where it fails, and change one thing at a time.

content.text: Zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot

A prompt with no examples is called **zero-shot**. One example makes it **one-shot**, and several make it **few-shot**. Start zero-shot with clear instructions. If the format or style is still wrong, add examples. Few-shot prompting is especially helpful for tasks like classification (“positive”, “negative”, “neutral”) and for matching a house style.
Prompts are not the whole story

Prompt engineering has limits. A model cannot know facts it was never given. If you need answers about your own documents, give it those documents (this is called retrieval, covered in the RAG course). If you need a guaranteed format, validate the answer in code. If an answer matters, a person should check it. Good prompts raise the quality, and testing and checking keep it there.

items: A prompt works best when it removes guesswork: role, task, context, rules, examples and output format.
Be specific, separate instructions from data, allow “I don’t know”, and iterate.
Examples are powerful, but watch for clashes between the rules and the examples.

content.text: In the next lesson you will learn more advanced techniques: step-by-step reasoning, prompt chains, and ways to combine several small prompts.

faqs.q: Do longer prompts always give better results?
faqs.a: No. A prompt should be as long as it needs to be. Extra, unclear or repeated instructions can confuse the model and cost more. Add only the details that change the answer.

faqs.q: Should I say please and thank you to the model?
faqs.a: It does not matter much for quality. A clear and polite tone is fine, but the facts, the task and the format are what make the difference.

faqs.q: What is the difference between zero-shot and few-shot prompting?
faqs.a: Zero-shot gives only instructions. Few-shot also includes a small number of examples of the input and the output you want, which helps the model copy the format and style.

faqs.q: Is prompt engineering a real job?
faqs.a: Writing and testing good prompts is a real skill, and it is part of many roles, such as developer, analyst and content specialist. Most of it is clear writing, careful testing and knowing what the task needs.

lessons.title: Advanced Prompting Techniques
lessons.description: Learn step-by-step reasoning, few-shot examples, self-checks and prompt chains, and build a chain runner where the output of each prompt feeds the next.

content.text: Basic prompts work well for short, clear tasks. But some tasks are bigger: analyse a resume against a job post, write a summary, check it for errors, and then rewrite it. If you put all of that into one giant prompt, the model may skip steps, mix them up or drop details. The answer is to use a few proven techniques. In this lesson you will learn four of them: asking for step-by-step reasoning, using examples well, asking the model to check its own work, and splitting a big job into a **prompt chain**. Then you will build a chain runner in the lab and watch the output of one step flow into the next.
Technique 1: ask for the steps

Models often do better on problems with several steps if they write out the steps before the final answer. This is called **chain-of-thought** prompting. When the model writes the steps, each step becomes part of the text that the next token is based on. So the reasoning is not hidden. It is on the page, where the model can use it and you can read it.

Example: “A forklift driver works 8 hours a day, 5 days a week, and is paid 150 rupees an hour. What does the driver earn in 4 weeks? Work through the steps, then give the final answer on a new line starting with ANSWER.” The model will write: 8 × 150 = 1,200 a day; 1,200 × 5 = 6,000 a week; 6,000 × 4 = 24,000. Then: ANSWER: 24,000 rupees. Without the instruction, a model might jump straight to a number and make a mistake.

Two cautions. First, the steps cost tokens, so use this when the task needs it, not for simple questions. Second, a model’s written reasoning is useful but is not a perfect picture of what happens inside it, so still check the final answer. Some newer models have reasoning built in and think before they answer. For those, a short clear task often works better than long instructions about how to think. Read the guide for the model you use.
Technique 2: use examples well
You met examples in lesson 8. Here are three tips that matter more as tasks get harder.

items: **Cover the variety.** If your inputs can be short, long, messy or empty, show one example of each kind.
**Show the hard case.** Include an example where the right answer is “none found” or “not enough information”. Otherwise the model learns that it must always find something.
**Keep the format identical.** The model copies the pattern closely, including small details like capital letters and punctuation.

content.text: Technique 3: ask for a check

A model can often find mistakes in text more easily than it can avoid them while writing. So a useful pattern is to produce a draft, then ask for a review against a clear list: “Check the summary below against the resume. List any claim that is not in the resume. If there are none, write OK.” You can do this in the same prompt or, better, as a separate step. A separate step gives the reviewer a fresh view and a focused job.
A review step is not a guarantee. The reviewer can also be wrong, and it may agree with a bad draft. Use it to catch common problems, and still test with real examples and check what matters.
Technique 4: prompt chaining
A **prompt chain** splits one big task into several small prompts. The output of one prompt is placed into the next. For a resume helper, a chain might be:

items: **Extract.** Read the resume and list the skills, tools and job titles.
**Match.** Compare that list with the job post and list what is missing.
**Rewrite.** Write three improved bullets that use the missing skills the person truly has.
**Check.** Review the bullets for invented facts and for length.

content.text: Why is this better than one big prompt?

items: **Each step is simple**, so the model does it better and you can write a short, clear prompt for it.
**You can test each step alone.** If the final answer is wrong, you can look at the output of each step and find where it went wrong.
**You can mix tools.** One step can use a small cheap model and another a strong one. A step can also be ordinary code, such as checking a format.
**You can stop early.** If the extract step finds no skills, there is no need to run the others.
**You can run steps in parallel** when they do not depend on each other.

content.text: The price is more calls, so more cost and delay, and more places where an error can enter and be passed on. A small mistake in step 1 can ruin step 3. So check the output of important steps, and keep the data passed between them short and clean.
How to pass data between steps

In a chain, each step is a **template**: a prompt with placeholders such as {{input}} for the original text and {{prev}} for the previous output. Before a step runs, the program replaces each placeholder with real text. Because the placeholders can name earlier steps, for example {{skills}}, a later step can use any earlier output and not only the last one.

Keep two safety rules in mind. First, wrap pasted data in tags so the model sees it as data. Second, remember that the output of one step becomes the input of the next. If an earlier output could contain text from an untrusted source, the next step may follow instructions hidden inside it. Lesson 11 returns to this.
Other useful patterns

items: **Role and audience switch.** Ask for the same content for different readers: a hiring manager, a new employee, a parent.
**Critique and revise.** Draft, critique with a rubric, revise once. More loops rarely help.
**Decompose then combine.** Ask the model first to list the parts of a problem, then solve each part, then combine.
**Ask for options.** For creative tasks, ask for five versions, then choose or ask for a ranking with reasons.
**Ask for missing information.** Tell the model: “If you need more information, ask me one question before answering.” This works well in chat.

items: Asking for steps helps with multi-step problems, but costs tokens and is not a perfect view of the model’s thinking.

faqs.q: What is chain-of-thought prompting?
faqs.a: It means asking the model to write out its reasoning steps before the final answer. It often improves results on tasks with several steps, such as maths or planning, because the steps become part of the text the model continues from.

faqs.q: When should I use a prompt chain instead of one prompt?
faqs.a: Use a chain when the task has clear stages, when one prompt becomes long or unreliable, or when you want to test and fix each stage on its own. For simple tasks one good prompt is cheaper and faster.

faqs.q: Do chains make answers always more accurate?
faqs.a: Not always. They often make results easier to control and debug, but each extra step adds cost and a chance for an error to pass on. Test the whole chain on real examples.

faqs.q: Can one step in a chain be normal code?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is a good idea. Steps such as checking a format, counting words or looking up a database record are better done in code than by a model.

content.text: When a person reads a model’s answer, small differences do not matter. “The score is about seventy” is fine. But when a program reads the answer, everything matters. Code expects a number, not the word “seventy”. It expects exactly the field names it was written for. A missing comma can crash the app. For this reason, when you build software on top of a model, you need **structured output**: answers in a fixed format, usually **JSON**, that code can read safely. In this lesson you will learn how to ask for JSON, why you must never trust it blindly, how to validate it against a schema, and how to build a repair loop. You will build the validator in the lab.
What is JSON?

JSON is a simple text format for data that almost every programming language can read. It has objects in curly braces with named fields, lists in square brackets, and values that can be text, numbers, true or false, or null. Example:

This is a small match report for a resume: a score, a verdict and a list of skills that are missing. Notice that text values are in double quotes, there is no comma after the last item, and names are in double quotes too. These small rules are exactly where models sometimes slip.
How to ask for JSON

items: **Show the shape.** Put an example of the exact JSON you want in the prompt, with the field names and the type of each value.
**Say what each field means.** “score: a whole number from 0 to 100.” “verdict: one of strong, partial or weak.”
**Limit the words.** “Return only the JSON, with no other text.” Models still sometimes add a friendly sentence or wrap the JSON in a code fence, so your code must be ready for that.
**Handle missing data.** Decide what to return when something is unknown: null, an empty list, or a special value. Say it in the prompt.
**Keep it small.** Ask for the fields you really need. Fewer fields means fewer mistakes.

content.text: Many model providers also offer features that force the output to follow a schema, sometimes called structured outputs or JSON mode, or the ability to make the model call a tool with a defined set of arguments. Use them when available, because they cut errors a lot. Even then, keep your own validation, because a valid shape does not mean the content is right: a score can be in range and still be wrong.
Why you must validate

Imagine your app reads the model’s answer and shows the score on a progress bar. One day the model returns “score”: 140. The bar breaks. Another day it returns “missing_skills”: “Zendesk”, a text and not a list, and your code that loops over the list fails or loops over letters. The answers look right to a human glance. But code needs checks, in the same way a form on a website checks an email address before saving it.

**Validation** means checking the data against rules before you use it. A **schema** is the description of those rules. For our match report the schema says: the answer must be an object; score is required and must be a whole number from 0 to 100; verdict is required and must be one of three values; missing_skills is required and must be a list of up to eight short texts.
Step 1: extract the JSON

Models often wrap JSON in other text: “Sure! Here is the result:” followed by the JSON, or a markdown code fence. A good first step is an **extractor** that finds the JSON in the text. A simple, careful way is to look for a code fence first, then find the first opening bracket and walk forward, counting brackets and ignoring brackets that appear inside quoted text, until the bracket closes. Then run the standard JSON parser on that piece. If the bracket never closes, the answer was cut off, and you should say so.
Step 2: check against the schema

Write a function that goes through the data and the schema together and returns a **list of problems** in plain words: “answer.score must be at most 100”, “answer.missing_skills must be a list”, “answer.verdict must be one of: strong, partial, weak”. A list of clear messages is more useful than a simple yes or no, because you can show it to a developer, log it, and, as the next step shows, send it back to the model.
Step 3: the repair loop

When validation fails, you have three choices: show an error, retry the same prompt, or **repair**. In a repair, you send a short follow-up message to the model, with the problems found, and ask for a corrected version: “Your JSON had these problems: answer.score must be at most 100. Return the corrected JSON only.” Because the model sees its earlier answer and the exact problems, it fixes them most of the time.

Always limit the loop, for example to two or three repairs. If the answer is still invalid after that, stop and handle the failure in a safe way: use a default, ask the user, or flag it for a person. A loop with no limit can run up your bill and never end.
Safe handling of the result

items: **Never run text from a model as code.** Parse it as data only.
**Check the content as well as the shape.** If the verdict says “strong” but the score is 5, something is wrong. Add rules that compare fields.
**Limit sizes.** A list of 10,000 items or a text of 50,000 characters can hurt your app.
**Log failures.** The rate of invalid answers is a quality number to watch over time.
**Keep secrets out.** Do not put passwords or private data into schemas or examples.

faqs.q: Why not just trust the model to return valid JSON?
faqs.a: Models usually do, but not always. They may add text around the JSON, miss a bracket, use the wrong type or invent field names. One bad answer can crash your app, so always parse and validate before using it.

faqs.q: What is a JSON schema?
faqs.a: It is a description of what valid data looks like: which fields exist, which are required, and what type, range or allowed values each has. Tools can use it to check data automatically. The lab uses a small schema format of its own for clarity.

faqs.q: How many repair attempts should I allow?
faqs.a: Usually one to three. Most fixable mistakes are fixed in the first repair. After that, stop and use a safe fallback so that a bad answer cannot cause an endless loop or a large bill.

faqs.q: Are structured output features from model providers enough?
faqs.a: They greatly reduce format errors, but they do not check whether the content is true or sensible. Keep your own checks for ranges, sizes and the relation between fields.
